title: Pentimento: Data Remanence in Cloud FPGAs
problem: Remote attackers can recover long-removed data from cloud FPGAs through bias temperature instability (BTI) side-channels. This 'pentimento' is imprinted on transistors through degradation patterns that can be measured using timing sensors.
motivation: Data remanence in shared cloud FPGAs poses a critical security risk, potentially exposing proprietary designs and cryptographic keys from previous users or marketplace designs.
method: Transistors in FPGAs accumulate damage (called bias temperature instability) as they process data, and this damage pattern encodes information about past computation. Attackers use time-to-digital converters—sensors that measure tiny timing differences in transistor behavior—to detect these patterns. These measurements reveal data that was previously processed, similar to how infrared imaging reveals old paintings hidden beneath new paint.
key_novelty: Transistor aging (bias temperature instability) in shared cloud FPGAs creates a side-channel—a hidden leak of information—that reveals previously processed data through timing measurements.
contributions: Discovery of FPGA pentimento vulnerability exploitable through BTI side-channels on cloud platforms
Development of time-to-digital converter based attack methodology
Extraction of proprietary details and keys from encrypted FPGA designs on AWS marketplace
Validation with AES key recovery on AWS F1 instances

metrics.accuracy: successful AES key recovery under threat model

primary_theme: Side-channel recovery of cloud FPGA data via BTI degradation
